decks.title: Cell: The Unit of Life — Part 1: Cell theory, the membrane and the endomembrane system
goals: State the cell theory and Virchow’s modification; compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and plant and animal cells
Describe the cell wall and plasmodesmata, and the fluid mosaic model with active and passive transport
Describe the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles and how they work together in secretion

slides.heading: The cell: the unit of life
slides.body_md: Part 1: the cell theory, the plasma membrane and the organelles that make and ship proteins.

visual.alt: Path from the discovery of cells to the cell theory, the membrane and the endomembrane system

slides.narration: Every living thing is made of cells. In this part we follow how cells were discovered, how the cell theory was framed, how the membrane controls traffic, and how a group of organelles cooperates to make and export proteins.

slides.heading: Discovery and the cell theory
slides.body_md: The cell theory was built step by step. **Schleiden and Schwann** proposed that all plants and animals are made of cells and their products; **Virchow** added that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula-e cellula*), which **modified** the theory.

rows: Saw box-like compartments in a slice of cork and named them cells
First saw living cells with a simple microscope
All plants are made of cells
All animals are made of cells; the cell theory

visual.alt: Table of the people who built the cell theory

slides.narration: Hooke named the cell from dead cork. Leeuwenhoek saw living ones. Brown found the nucleus. Schleiden and Schwann said that plants and animals are made of cells. Sixteen years later, Virchow completed the idea: every cell comes from an earlier cell.

slides.heading: Size and shape of cells
slides.body_md: Cell size ranges from the tiny **Mycoplasma** to the **ostrich egg**, the largest single cell; shape matches function.

rows: Lives as a parasite with few needs
Branched, some over a metre long
Lines a gut and absorbs food

visual.alt: Table of cell sizes and shapes with their functions

slides.narration: Cells vary widely in size and shape. Tiny Mycoplasma and huge egg cells are the extremes. A red blood cell is a flat disc, a nerve cell is long and branched, and a muscle cell is a spindle, each shape suiting its job.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: why most cells are small
slides.body_md: Three model cells are cubes of side 2, 4 and 8 micrometres. Compare their surface area to volume ratio, and say what happens if the large cell's volume is divided into small cells.
bullets: Surface area is six times the side squared: 24, 96 and 384 square micrometres. Volume is the side cubed: 8, 64 and 512 cubic micrometres.
Ratio of surface to volume: 3, 1.5 and 0.75. The ratio falls as the cell grows.
The large cube holds 64 small cubes. Their total surface is 1536, which is 4 times the 384 of the large cube.
Many small cells exchange materials more quickly than one large cell of the same volume.

visual.alt: Worked table: ratios 3, 1.5, 0.75

slides.narration: As a cell grows, its volume rises faster than its surface. So the surface that must pass in food and oxygen becomes small compared with the cytoplasm to be served. Dividing the same volume into many small cells restores a large surface.

slides.heading: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
slides.body_md: The two basic cell types differ in organisation, not in the molecules of life.

rows: True nucleus with a double envelope
Linear, with histone proteins, several chromosomes

visual.alt: Table comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

slides.narration: A prokaryote has its genetic material lying free in the cytoplasm and has no membrane-bound organelles. A eukaryote keeps its linear chromosomes inside a nucleus and divides its work among organelles. Bacteria are prokaryotes; protists, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotes.

slides.heading: Plant cell and animal cell
slides.body_md: Both are eukaryotic, but they differ in several structures.

visual.alt: Table comparing plant and animal cells

slides.narration: A plant cell has a cellulose wall, plastids and a large central vacuole. An animal cell lacks these but has centrioles. They also store food differently: starch in plants and glycogen in animals.

slides.heading: Quick check: the cell theory
slides.body_md: Which idea did Virchow add to the cell theory?
slides.narration: Quick check. What did Virchow add to the idea of Schleiden and Schwann?

slides.heading: Cell wall and plasmodesmata
slides.body_md: The **cell wall** is a non-living, rigid outer layer in plants, algae and fungi. It protects the cell, gives it shape and prevents bursting. **Plasmodesmata** are cytoplasmic threads that pass through the walls and connect neighbouring cells.

rows: Cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin and proteins; primary wall and, in some cells, a secondary wall
Calcium pectate that cements neighbouring cells
Algal walls: cellulose, galactans, mannans, minerals; fungal walls: chitin
Channels lined by the plasma membrane and joined by a strand of endoplasmic reticulum; carry water, ions and small molecules between cells

visual.alt: Table of the cell wall and plasmodesmata

slides.narration: The wall is the protective outer coat of plant, algal and fungal cells. Neighbouring cells are cemented by the middle lamella, yet remain in contact because plasmodesmata link their cytoplasm through tiny gaps in the wall.

slides.heading: The fluid mosaic model
slides.body_md: Singer and Nicolson proposed the **fluid mosaic model** in nineteen seventy-two: a **quasi-fluid lipid bilayer** in which **proteins float like a mosaic**.

slides.narration: Phospholipid molecules have water-loving heads facing outwards and water-hating tails inside. Integral proteins span the bilayer and peripheral proteins lie on its surface. Cholesterol adds stability. Because lipids and proteins can move sideways, the membrane is fluid.

slides.heading: Passive and active transport
slides.body_md: Substances cross the membrane without energy (**passive**) or with energy from ATP (**active**).

rows: Down a gradient, carrier or channel, no ATP, saturates
Glucose entering a red blood cell
Water down its gradient across the membrane
Against a gradient, carrier, uses ATP

visual.alt: Table of passive and active transport

slides.narration: Passive movements need no energy because they go downhill along a gradient. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier proteins but is still passive. Active transport pushes substances uphill and uses energy from ATP, as in the sodium potassium pump.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a transport graph
slides.body_md: The graph shows the rate of entry of a sugar into a cell by simple diffusion and by a carrier. The carrier's maximum is 60 units a minute, reached only at very high concentration.
bullets: At a concentration of 40 units the carrier moves 40 units a minute, but diffusion only 10.
Doubling the concentration from 100 to 200 raises the carrier rate by only 4.5 units (9 percent), yet diffusion rises by 25 units. The carrier is already at 90.8 percent of its maximum.
The carrier curve levels off because every carrier molecule is busy: facilitated diffusion is specific and saturable. The straight line shows no limit.

slides.heading: ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles
slides.body_md: Each organelle of the system has its own job.

rows: Flattened sacs with ribosomes, joined to the nuclear envelope
Makes proteins for secretion and for membranes
Stack of flattened cisternae, with a cis and a trans face
Modifies, sorts and packages; forms lysosomes
Single membrane (tonoplast) enclosing sap or water
Stores, maintains turgor, removes water in protists

visual.alt: Table of the endomembrane organelles

slides.narration: The rough endoplasmic reticulum makes protein and the smooth type makes lipids. The Golgi complex packages and sends products out. Lysosomes digest, and vacuoles store water and wastes and keep plant cells firm.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cell theory: all organisms are made of cells; cells arise from pre-existing cells (Virchow).
Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; plant cells have a wall, plastids and a large vacuole.
Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson): lipid bilayer with floating proteins.
Passive transport needs no ATP; active transport does. Carriers: uniport, symport, antiport.
Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, vacuoles.

visual.alt: Summary table of key points

slides.narration: To recap: cells come from cells; prokaryotes and eukaryotes differ in organisation; the membrane is a fluid mosaic; transport can be passive or active; and linked organelles make, pack and export proteins.

notes.title: Cell: The Unit of Life — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Historical aspects, cell theory, size and shape; prokaryotic and eukaryotic, plant and animal cells
sections.body_md:
**History.** **Robert Hooke** (1665 saw box-like compartments in a thin slice of cork and called them **cells**; he saw only dead cell walls. **Anton van Leeuwenhoek** (1674) was the first to see **living** cells. **Robert Brown** (1831) discovered the **nucleus**. **Matthias Schleiden** (1838, plants) and **Theodor Schwann** (1839, animals) proposed that the bodies of plants and animals are made of cells and their products. **Rudolf Virchow** (1855) stated ***omnis cellula-e cellula***: new cells arise only from **pre-existing cells**, which **modified** the cell theory.

**Cell theory (as modified by Virchow):** (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and their products; (ii) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; (iii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

**Size and shape.** Cells range from about 0.3 µm (*Mycoplasma*, the smallest) through bacteria (a few µm) and the human red blood cell (about 7 µm) to the ostrich egg, the largest single cell; some nerve cells are over a metre long. Shapes include discs, spindles, columns, cubes and branched forms, and each suits a function. Size is limited by the **surface-to-volume ratio**: for cubes of side 2, 4, 8 µm the ratio falls from 3 to 1.5 to 0.75, so a large cell is poorly served by its surface.

**Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.** Prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria, *Mycoplasma*) have a **nucleoid** with circular naked DNA, **no membrane-bound organelles** and **70S ribosomes**; they divide by binary fission. Eukaryotes (protists, fungi, plants, animals) have a **true nucleus**, linear DNA with histones, membrane-bound organelles and **80S ribosomes** (70S in mitochondria and plastids).

**Plant and animal cells.** A plant cell has a **cellulose cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole**, lacks centrioles (in higher plants) and stores **starch**, dividing by a **cell plate**. An animal cell has no wall or plastids, has **centrioles** and small vacuoles, stores **glycogen** and divides by a **furrow**.

key_terms.definition_md: Organisms are made of cells; the cell is the unit of structure and function; cells arise from cells.
Virchow’s statement that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.
Cell with no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
Cell with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

sections.heading: 2. Cell wall, plasmodesmata and the plasma membrane; transport
sections.body_md:
**Cell wall.** A non-living, rigid layer outside the plasma membrane of plants, algae and fungi. In plants it is made of **cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin and proteins**, with a **primary wall** and sometimes a **secondary wall**; **calcium pectate** forms the **middle lamella** that holds neighbouring cells together. Algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals; fungal walls contain **chitin**. The wall gives **shape and protection** and prevents bursting in hypotonic surroundings. **Plasmodesmata** are cytoplasmic channels through the wall, lined by the plasma membrane and often traversed by a strand of endoplasmic reticulum; they link the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

**Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).** The membrane is a **quasi-fluid bilayer of phospholipids** whose polar heads face the watery surroundings and whose non-polar tails face each other; **proteins** are embedded like a mosaic — **integral** proteins span or penetrate the bilayer and **peripheral** proteins lie on a surface. **Cholesterol** lies among the tails, and **carbohydrate chains** on proteins and lipids face outwards. The lateral movement of lipids and proteins (fluidity) permits **endocytosis, secretion, cell growth, division and formation of junctions**.

**Transport.** **Passive** movement needs no ATP: **simple diffusion** of small non-polar molecules, **facilitated diffusion** through specific **carrier or channel proteins** (rate rises and then **saturates**; example: glucose into a red blood cell) and **osmosis**. **Active transport** moves a substance **against its gradient** with a carrier and **ATP** (example: the **sodium–potassium pump**). Carriers are **uniport** (one substance, one way), **symport** (two substances, same way) or **antiport** (two substances, opposite ways). In the model transport graph the carrier gives 20 units at a concentration of 10 and levels off near its maximum of 60, while diffusion rises as a straight line.

key_terms.definition_md: Cytoplasmic channels that pass through plant cell walls.
Membrane as a fluid lipid bilayer with a mosaic of proteins (Singer and Nicolson).
Passive movement through a specific carrier or channel; saturable; no ATP.
Carrier that moves two substances in opposite directions.

sections.heading: 3. Endomembrane system: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles
sections.body_md:
The **endomembrane system** consists of organelles whose functions are coordinated: the **ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles** (mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included because their functions are not coordinated with these).

- **Endoplasmic reticulum.** A network of tubules and flattened sacs (cisternae) continuous with the nuclear envelope. **Rough ER** has **ribosomes** on its outer face and makes **proteins for secretion and for membranes**; **smooth ER** has none and makes **lipids and steroids**, and detoxifies drugs.
- **Golgi complex** (Camillo Golgi). A stack of flat cisternae near the nucleus with a **cis (forming) face** receiving vesicles from the ER and a **trans (maturing) face** that sends them out; it **modifies, sorts and packages** products, adds carbohydrate, and forms **lysosomes**.
- **Lysosomes.** Single-membrane vesicles with **hydrolytic enzymes** (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) active at **acidic pH**; digest food and worn-out organelles (“**suicide bags**”).
- **Vacuoles.** Single-membrane sacs; in plants a large central vacuole bounded by the **tonoplast** holds sap, maintains **turgor** and stores waste; **contractile vacuoles** in protists expel water; **food vacuoles** digest food.

**Coordination in secretion.** A protein made on the rough ER enters its cavity, is carried by a **vesicle** to the **cis face**, modified through the stack, leaves the **trans face** in vesicles, and either is **secreted** at the plasma membrane or forms a **lysosome**.

sections.heading: 4. Mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes and microbodies
sections.body_md:
**Mitochondria** are double-membraned, sausage-shaped organelles. The **outer membrane** is smooth; the **inner membrane** is folded into **cristae** that increase the surface and carry the particles that make **ATP**; the **matrix** contains respiratory enzymes, **circular DNA** and **70S ribosomes**. They are the sites of **aerobic respiration** and divide by fission.

**Plastids** are double-membraned organelles of plants and algae. **Chloroplasts** contain **chlorophyll**; the inner membrane system is a set of **thylakoids** stacked into **grana** and joined by **stroma lamellae**; the **stroma** has enzymes for making carbohydrates and proteins, DNA and 70S ribosomes. **Chromoplasts** hold **carotenoids** and give yellow, orange and red colours. **Leucoplasts** are colourless stores: **amyloplasts** (starch), **elaioplasts** (oils and fats), **aleuroplasts** (proteins).

**Ribosomes** are non-membranous particles of **rRNA and protein**, the sites of protein synthesis: **70S** (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes, mitochondria and plastids; **80S** (60S + 40S) in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes, free or on the rough ER. (S, the Svedberg unit, measures sedimentation rate, so subunit values do not simply add.)

**Microbodies** are single-membrane vesicles with enzymes: **peroxisomes** (catalase; break down hydrogen peroxide) and **glyoxysomes** (germinating fatty seeds; convert fat to carbohydrate).

sections.heading: 5. Cytoskeleton; cilia, flagella and centrioles
sections.body_md:
The **cytoskeleton** is a network of protein filaments: **microfilaments** (actin; thinnest; contraction, shape, cytoplasmic streaming), **intermediate filaments** (fibrous proteins such as keratin; strong mechanical support) and **microtubules** (tubulin; hollow; spindle, cilia, flagella, centrioles; guide the movement of vesicles).

**Cilia and flagella** are hair-like projections of the plasma membrane. **Cilia** are short and numerous and beat like oars; **flagella** are long and few and propel the cell, as in a sperm. Each has a core, the **axoneme**, of **nine peripheral doublet microtubules and two central single microtubules** (the **9 + 2** arrangement, 20 microtubules in all), joined by **radial spokes**, and arises from a **basal body**.

**Centrioles** form the **centrosome** (two centrioles at right angles) in animal cells and some lower plants; each has **nine peripheral triplets** of microtubules in a cartwheel with **no central pair** (27 microtubules). They organise the **spindle and asters** in cell division and give rise to basal bodies.

sections.heading: 6. Nucleus: envelope, chromatin, nucleolus; chromosomes
sections.body_md:
The **nucleus** (Robert Brown, 1831) controls the cell. The **nuclear envelope** is two membranes separated by a **perinuclear space**, perforated by **nuclear pores** that control the passage of RNA and proteins; the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER. The **nucleoplasm** contains **chromatin**, DNA with histone proteins: **euchromatin** is loosely packed, lightly stained and transcriptionally **active**; **heterochromatin** is densely packed, darkly stained and **inactive**. The **nucleolus** is a dense, **non-membrane-bound** body, the site of **rRNA synthesis and assembly of ribosome subunits**; it is large in cells that make much protein.

**Chromosomes** show a **centromere** (primary constriction) bearing disc-shaped **kinetochores** to which spindle fibres attach. By its position they are: **metacentric** (middle, equal arms), **submetacentric** (slightly off the middle, one arm longer), **acrocentric** (near one end, one very short arm) and **telocentric** (at the end). Some chromosomes have a **secondary constriction** that cuts off a small **satellite**. In the model data, short arms of 9, 6, 3, 0 µm on a total of 20 µm give metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric, telocentric chromosomes. (Strict cut-off values for the types differ between books; the position of the centromere is what the syllabus asks.)

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving Virchow’s statement as the whole cell theory (it modified it: cells arise from cells).
- Saying facilitated diffusion needs ATP (it does not); or that active transport goes down the gradient (it goes against).
- Labelling the Golgi cis face as the one that releases vesicles (the trans face does).
- Calling lysosomes and peroxisomes the same (lysosomes: hydrolytic enzymes; peroxisomes: catalase).
- Writing 9 + 0 for a cilium (it is 9 + 2; 9 + 0 triplets is the centriole and basal body).
- Mixing up acrocentric (near one end) and telocentric (at the end).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a scientist, a term, a type of plastid, the cilium pattern, a chromosome type, give-a-reason and analogy.
- 2–3-mark questions: prokaryotic versus eukaryotic or plant versus animal in a table; active transport versus facilitated diffusion; ER and Golgi; chromosome types.
- 5-mark questions in parts: fluid mosaic model with a labelled diagram; endomembrane coordination; mitochondrion and chloroplast diagrams.

questions.stem_md: Which idea did Rudolf Virchow add to the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann?

options.text_md: All new cells arise from pre-existing cells
All plants are made of cells
All animals are made of cells
The cell is bounded by a membrane

questions.solution_md: Omnis cellula-e cellula: cells come only from cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement separates active transport from facilitated diffusion?

options.text_md: Active transport moves a substance against its concentration gradient and uses ATP
Only active transport needs a protein in the membrane
Only facilitated diffusion is specific for the substance it moves
Only facilitated diffusion can move a substance across a lipid bilayer

questions.solution_md: Both use carrier proteins and both are specific; only active transport works uphill with ATP — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packs proteins into vesicles for secretion?
questions.solution_md: Proteins from the rough ER are finished and dispatched by the Golgi complex — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which plastid stores oils and fats in the cells of an oil-rich seed?
questions.solution_md: Elaioplasts store oils; amyloplasts store starch and aleuroplasts proteins — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a cross-section of a cilium, the microtubules of the axoneme are arranged as

options.text_md: nine outer triplets around two central microtubules
nine outer doublets around two central single microtubules
nine outer doublets with no central microtubules
two outer doublets around nine central microtubules

questions.solution_md: The axoneme has the 9 + 2 pattern — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A chromosome has its centromere at the extreme end. It is called
questions.solution_md: A terminal centromere makes the chromosome telocentric — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In 1665 Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork under a microscope. What did he actually see?

options.text_md: Empty box-like compartments, the walls of dead cells
Chains of bacteria between the cells

questions.solution_md: Cork is dead tissue; Hooke saw only the cell walls — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A model cell is a cube of side 4 micrometres. When it grows to a cube of side 8 micrometres, its surface area to volume ratio

options.text_md: stays at 1.5, because the shape is unchanged
falls to a quarter, from 1.5 to 0.375

questions.solution_md: Surface area rises fourfold (96 to 384) but volume eightfold (64 to 512), so the ratio halves — option (a).

questions.solution_md: A chitin wall with a true nucleus fits a fungus, not a bacterium, an alga (cellulose wall) or Amoeba (no wall) — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Ribosomes occur in all cells; the other structures are eukaryotic only — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A cell cannot arise from non-living matter in a sterilised, sealed nutrient broth.

**Reason (R):** According to Virchow, all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and with no living cell present none can appear, as Virchow’s statement predicts — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Most cells of a multicellular body are microscopic.

answer.model_answer_md: A small cell has a **large surface-to-volume ratio**, so materials enter and wastes leave quickly enough to serve all of its cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: Surface-to-volume ratio.

marking_scheme.step: Large surface-to-volume ratio gives fast exchange

questions.stem_md: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 5 micrometres. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio.
questions.solution_md: Surface area $= 6 \times 5^2 = 150$; volume $= 5^3 = 125$; ratio $= \dfrac{150}{125} = 1.2$.

questions.stem_md: A cube-shaped cell of side 6 micrometres is divided into cubes of side 3 micrometres with the same total volume. By what factor does the total surface area increase?
questions.solution_md: Number of small cubes $= \dfrac{6^3}{3^3} = 8$; their total surface $= 8 \times 54 = 432$; the large cube has 216; factor $= 2$.

marking_scheme.step: Eight small cubes and their total surface

questions.stem_md: A student writes: “Virchow proposed the cell theory.” Correct her statement by naming the scientists who proposed the theory and stating what Virchow added.

answer.model_answer_md: The cell theory was proposed by **Schleiden and Schwann** (1838–1839): all plants and animals are made of **cells and their products**. **Virchow** (1855) **modified** it by stating that **new cells arise only from pre-existing cells** (*omnis cellula-e cellula*).

questions.solution_md: Schleiden and Schwann; Virchow’s addition.

marking_scheme.step: Virchow: cells arise from pre-existing cells

questions.stem_md: A bacterium and a yeast cell are both unicellular. Tabulate three structural differences between them, naming the type of cell each is.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **bacterium** is **prokaryotic**; the **yeast** is **eukaryotic**.

| Feature | Bacterium | Yeast |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | No envelope; **nucleoid** | **True nucleus** with envelope |
| DNA | Circular, naked | Linear, with **histones** |
| Organelles | **None** membrane-bound | Mitochondria, ER, Golgi complex |

questions.solution_md: Table of three differences.

questions.stem_md: A student sees under the microscope one cell with a cellulose wall and one without. Distinguish a plant cell from an animal cell on the basis of cell wall, vacuole and reserve food.

answer.model_answer_md: A **plant cell** has a **cellulose cell wall**, a **large central vacuole** and stores **starch**; an **animal cell** has **no wall**, only **small, temporary vacuoles** and stores **glycogen**. The plant cell also has plastids and divides by a cell plate, while the animal cell has centrioles and divides by a furrow.

questions.solution_md: Wall, vacuole, reserve food.

questions.stem_md: A piece of soft fruit tissue is soaked in a chemical that dissolves calcium pectate, and the cells fall apart. Which layer was dissolved?
questions.solution_md: Calcium pectate is the cement of the middle lamella — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of the plasma membrane, which letter marks a peripheral protein?
questions.solution_md: D lies on the surface without penetrating the bilayer — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student measures the uptake of a sugar by two kinds of cell at rising outside concentrations. In cell P the uptake rises steadily without limit; in cell Q it rises and then levels off. What do the results suggest?

options.text_md: Cell P takes in the sugar by simple diffusion and cell Q by a carrier.
Cell P uses a carrier and cell Q simple diffusion.
Cell Q has no plasma membrane.

questions.solution_md: A limit means a finite number of carriers (facilitated diffusion); no limit means plain diffusion — option (a).

questions.solution_md: Two substances moving together in one direction means symport — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A pump in the plasma membrane uses ATP to move sodium ions out of a cell while bringing potassium ions in. Which two terms describe it?
questions.solution_md: It works against gradients with ATP and moves two ions in opposite directions — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rate of facilitated diffusion stops rising when the outside concentration is very high.

**Reason (R):** Facilitated diffusion uses ATP to push molecules against a concentration gradient.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true because all carriers are occupied, but the reason is false: facilitated diffusion is passive and uses no ATP — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A plant cell kept in pure water does not burst.

**Reason (R):** A plant cell has a large central vacuole.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the rigid cell wall, not the vacuole, resists the swelling — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Proteins can drift sideways within the plasma membrane.

answer.model_answer_md: The lipid bilayer is **quasi-fluid**, so the lipids and the proteins embedded in it can move laterally.

questions.solution_md: Fluid bilayer.

questions.stem_md: A carrier follows $v = \dfrac{V_{\max} S}{K + S}$ with $V_{\max} = 60$ units a minute and $K = 20$. Find the rate at an outside concentration $S = 60$.
questions.solution_md: $v = \dfrac{60 \times 60}{20 + 60} = \dfrac{3600}{80} = 45$ units per minute.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish active transport from facilitated diffusion, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Active transport** moves a substance **against its concentration gradient** using a carrier and **energy from ATP**; example: the **sodium–potassium pump**. **Facilitated diffusion** moves a substance **down its gradient** through a carrier or channel with **no ATP**; example: **glucose entering a red blood cell**.

questions.solution_md: Gradient and ATP; two examples.

marking_scheme.step: Facilitated: down gradient, no ATP, example

questions.stem_md: Explain how the fluid mosaic model accounts for (i) the selective permeability of the membrane and (ii) the ability of a cell to take in a droplet of fluid by forming a vesicle.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **hydrophobic core** of the bilayer blocks charged and polar substances, while **proteins** (carriers and channels) let specific substances through, so the membrane is **selectively permeable**. (ii) Because the lipids and proteins are **fluid**, a patch of membrane can bend, enclose the droplet and **pinch off as a vesicle** without losing its continuity.

questions.solution_md: Hydrophobic core and proteins; fluidity.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. [2]
(b) State who proposed the model and in which year, and name its two main kinds of molecule. [1]
(c) Explain how the fluid nature of the membrane helps a cell. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a **phospholipid bilayer** with **heads outside and tails inside**; **integral proteins** spanning it and **peripheral proteins** on a surface; **cholesterol** among the tails; **carbohydrate chains** on the outer face.

(b) **Singer and Nicolson**, **1972**; the molecules are **lipids** (mainly phospholipids) and **proteins**.

(c) Fluidity lets lipids and proteins **move laterally**, so the membrane can **form vesicles** (endocytosis and secretion), **change shape**, **grow**, **divide** with the cell and **form junctions**.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; proposers; fluidity.

questions.stem_md: Plasma cells of the immune system secrete large amounts of antibody protein. Which organelle would be especially extensive in them?
questions.solution_md: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes of the rough ER — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Liver cells of a patient who has taken a sleeping drug for months show a marked increase in one organelle, which helps to detoxify the drug. This organelle is most likely the
questions.solution_md: Smooth ER enzymes detoxify drugs — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A drug raises the pH inside the lysosomes of a cell from about 5 to about 7.5. What is the most immediate effect?

options.text_md: Lysosomes stop receiving vesicles from the Golgi complex at once.
Lysosomal enzymes work poorly, so digestion of engulfed material slows down.
The cell begins to make more ribosomes.

questions.solution_md: Lysosomal hydrolases are active at an acidic pH — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The hydrolytic enzymes of a lysosome do not normally digest the rest of the cell.

answer.model_answer_md: The enzymes are **enclosed by a single membrane** and work best at the **acidic pH** inside the lysosome, so they are kept away from the cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: Enclosed by a membrane.

marking_scheme.step: Enclosed by a membrane, acidic pH inside

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the Golgi complex and name the face through which material enters it.

answer.model_answer_md: The Golgi complex **modifies** proteins and lipids (for example by adding carbohydrate), then **sorts and packs** them into **vesicles** for secretion; it also **forms lysosomes**. Material enters through the **cis (forming) face**.

questions.solution_md: Two functions; cis face.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and say how it differs in structure from the rough type.

answer.model_answer_md: The smooth ER **makes lipids and steroid hormones** and **detoxifies drugs and poisons**. It is **tubular** and has **no ribosomes** on its surface, whereas the rough ER is made of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes.

questions.solution_md: Two functions; no ribosomes.

questions.stem_md: A plasma cell secretes an antibody protein. Describe, in order, how the protein travels from its synthesis to its release.

answer.model_answer_md: It is made by **ribosomes on the rough ER** and enters the **ER cavity**. A **transport vesicle** carries it to the **cis face of the Golgi complex**, where it is **modified** as it passes through the cisternae. Vesicles bud from the **trans face** and fuse with the **plasma membrane**, releasing the antibody.

questions.solution_md: Rough ER, vesicle, Golgi, vesicle, membrane.

questions.stem_md: Explain how lysosomes are related to the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi complex, and why these organelles are described together as a system.

answer.model_answer_md: The **lysosomal enzymes** are proteins made on the **rough ER**. They are carried in vesicles to the **Golgi complex**, which packs them into vesicles that bud off as **lysosomes**. Since each step passes material to the next by **vesicles** and their functions are **coordinated**, the ER, Golgi complex and lysosomes (and vacuoles) form one **endomembrane system**.

questions.solution_md: ER to Golgi to lysosome; coordination.

marking_scheme.step: Enzymes made on the rough ER
Linked by vesicles, so one system

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is the endomembrane system? Name its four components. [1]
(b) Describe the structure of the Golgi complex and state its role in secretion. [2]
(c) Describe the structure and function of a lysosome. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **endomembrane system** is the group of membranous organelles whose functions are **coordinated**: the **endoplasmic reticulum**, **Golgi complex**, **lysosomes** and **vacuoles**.

(b) The Golgi complex is a **stack of flattened cisternae** with a convex **cis (forming) face** that receives vesicles from the ER and a concave **trans (maturing) face**. It **modifies, sorts and packs** proteins and lipids into vesicles and sends them to the plasma membrane or to form lysosomes.

(c) A lysosome is a **single-membrane vesicle** filled with **hydrolytic enzymes** (lipases, proteases and carbohydrases) that work at **acidic pH**. It **digests** food taken in and **worn-out organelles**, so it is called a “suicide bag”.

questions.solution_md: Definition; Golgi; lysosome.

questions.stem_md: The heart muscle cells of a mouse work without rest, and their mitochondria have unusually numerous cristae. What does this feature provide?

options.text_md: More space in the outer membrane for DNA
A larger matrix for ribosomes only
A larger surface of inner membrane for the particles that make ATP
Extra pores for the entry of nuclear RNA

questions.solution_md: Cristae increase the inner membrane surface carrying the ATP-making particles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student breaks open chloroplasts and removes all the thylakoid membranes. Which activity of the chloroplast would be lost first?

options.text_md: Making carbohydrate from carbon dioxide in the stroma
Synthesis of proteins on the 70S ribosomes
Trapping of light energy by chlorophyll

questions.solution_md: Chlorophyll sits in the thylakoids; the stroma enzymes and ribosomes are left behind — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A green tomato turns red as it ripens. Which change in its cells best explains the colour?

options.text_md: Chloroplasts change into chromoplasts rich in carotenoids

questions.solution_md: Ripening converts chloroplasts into chromoplasts with red carotenoid pigment — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a germinating castor seed, stored fat is converted into sugar for the growing seedling. Which microbody carries out this conversion?
questions.solution_md: Glyoxysomes of fatty seeds change fat into carbohydrate — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An antibiotic stops protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes but not on 80S ribosomes. Which part of a human cell could it still affect?

options.text_md: The rough ER, because its ribosomes are 70S
The nucleolus, because it makes 70S subunits
No part, because human cells have no ribosomes
The mitochondria, because they contain 70S ribosomes

questions.solution_md: Cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, but mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is thrown into folds called cristae.

**Reason (R):** Cristae increase the surface for the enzymes and particles of ATP formation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the reason explains the folding — option (a).

answer.model_answer_md: **Crista** (cristae).

questions.solution_md: Crista.

questions.solution_md: $7.5 \times \dfrac{0.5}{3} = 1.25$ micrometres.

questions.stem_md: State two structural features of a mitochondrion that suit it to producing ATP, and say how each helps.

answer.model_answer_md: The **inner membrane is folded into cristae**, which gives a **large surface** for the ATP-making particles. The **matrix contains the enzymes of respiration**, so the reactions that feed the particles take place close to them.

questions.solution_md: Cristae; matrix enzymes.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts by their pigment and function.

answer.model_answer_md: **Chloroplasts** contain **chlorophyll** (with carotenoids) and carry out **photosynthesis**. **Chromoplasts** contain **carotenoids** and other fat-soluble pigments and give **yellow, orange or red** colours to petals and fruits. **Leucoplasts** are **colourless** and **store food**: amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts oils and aleuroplasts proteins.

questions.solution_md: Pigment and function of each.

questions.stem_md: Compare peroxisomes and glyoxysomes in terms of the cells in which they are found, their enzymes and their function.

answer.model_answer_md: **Peroxisomes** occur in **many cells**, such as leaf cells, and contain **catalase**, which **breaks down hydrogen peroxide** (and which, in leaves, works with chloroplasts and mitochondria in photorespiration). **Glyoxysomes** occur in **germinating fatty seeds**, contain enzymes of the **glyoxylate cycle**, and **convert stored fat into carbohydrate**. Both are single-membrane microbodies.

questions.solution_md: Site, enzymes, function.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the ultrastructure of a mitochondrion. [2]
(b) Draw a labelled diagram of a chloroplast. [2]
(c) State one structural feature that is common to the two organelles. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** an oval with a smooth **outer membrane**, an **inner membrane** folded into **cristae**, and the **matrix** inside; optionally circular DNA and ribosomes.

(b) **Diagram:** a **double envelope** around a fluid **stroma**; **grana** (stacks of **thylakoids**) joined by **stroma lamellae**; optionally DNA and ribosomes.

questions.solution_md: Two diagrams; common feature.

synthesise lipids on the smooth ER

The bone marrow of a rat

questions.solution_md: $9 \times 3 = 27$ per basal body; $180 \times 27 = 4860$.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Cells of the outer layer of the skin are rich in intermediate filaments.

answer.model_answer_md: These cells face constant **stretching and rubbing**, and intermediate filaments such as **keratin** are **tough and give mechanical strength**.

questions.solution_md: Mechanical strength.

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of filament of the cytoskeleton in order of increasing thickness, and name the protein that forms the thinnest and the thickest.

answer.model_answer_md: In order of thickness: **microfilaments**, **intermediate filaments** and **microtubules**. The thinnest, the microfilament, is made of **actin**; the thickest, the microtubule, is made of **tubulin**.

questions.solution_md: Order; actin; tubulin.

questions.stem_md: Describe the arrangement of microtubules in a cross-section of a cilium and name the structure from which it arises.

answer.model_answer_md: A cross-section shows **nine peripheral doublet microtubules** around **two central single microtubules** (the **9 + 2** pattern), joined by **radial spokes** and enclosed by the plasma membrane. The cilium arises from a **basal body**.

questions.solution_md: 9 + 2; basal body.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate cilia from flagella in three ways, and state what is common to their internal structure.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cilia** are **short and numerous** and beat like oars; **flagella** are **long and few** and move in a wave-like way to push the cell. Cilia mainly **move fluid past a cell or move small cells**, whereas flagella **propel the whole cell**, as in a sperm. Both have the same **9 + 2 axoneme** and arise from a **basal body**.

questions.solution_md: Length and number; movement; common structure.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Genes lying in heterochromatin are generally not expressed.

answer.model_answer_md: Heterochromatin is **tightly packed**, so the enzymes that **transcribe** the DNA cannot reach the genes.

questions.stem_md: A chromosome 18 micrometres long has its centromere 4 micrometres from one end. Name its type, giving a reason, and state the length of its long arm.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **acrocentric**, because the centromere lies **near one end**, leaving a very short arm (4 micrometres, about 22 percent of the length). The long arm is 18 − 4 = **14 micrometres**.

questions.solution_md: Acrocentric; long arm 14.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the nuclear envelope and state the role of the nuclear pores.

answer.model_answer_md: The **nuclear envelope** is made of **two membranes** separated by a **perinuclear space**; the outer membrane is **continuous with the rough ER** and may carry ribosomes. It is perforated by **nuclear pores**, which **control the passage** of RNA, ribosome subunits and proteins between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: Two membranes; space; pores.

marking_scheme.step: Outer membrane joined to rough ER

questions.stem_md: A cytologist sees four chromosomes of equal length. Their short arms are 9, 6, 3 and 0 micrometres on a total of 20 micrometres. Classify each and state where its centromere lies.

answer.model_answer_md: The 9 + 11 chromosome is **metacentric**, with the centromere **near the middle**. The 6 + 14 chromosome is **submetacentric**, with the centromere **a little off the middle**. The 3 + 17 chromosome is **acrocentric**, with it **near one end**, and the 0 + 20 chromosome is **telocentric**, with it at the **very end**.

questions.solution_md: Four types with positions.

questions.passage_md:
A tissue from a mouse kidney was homogenised and spun at increasing speeds. Four marker enzymes were assayed in each fraction (units of activity). Succinate dehydrogenase marks mitochondria, glucose-6-phosphatase the endoplasmic reticulum, acid phosphatase lysosomes and catalase peroxisomes.

| Enzyme | Nuclear pellet | Heavy pellet | Microsome pellet | Supernatant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Succinate dehydrogenase | 30 | 420 | 35 | 15 |
| Acid phosphatase | 20 | 260 | 20 | 200 |
| Glucose-6-phosphatase | 25 | 40 | 380 | 55 |
| Catalase | 10 | 90 | 30 | 70 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 84 %

**(b)** (b) The microsome pellet: broken pieces of ER close up into small vesicles that settle only at high speed.

**(c)** (i) Some **lysosomes burst** when the tissue was **homogenised**, so their enzymes were **released into the soluble fraction**. This shows that a **lysosome is a membrane-bound sac** that normally keeps its enzymes inside.

**OR** (ii) The heavy pellet also holds **52 percent of the acid phosphatase** (lysosomes) and **45 percent of the catalase** (peroxisomes), so it contains **lysosomes and peroxisomes** along with the mitochondria.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{420}{500} \times 100 = 84$ percent.

**(b)** Glucose-6-phosphatase is richest (76 percent) in the microsome pellet — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Broken lysosomes.

(ii) Other markers present.

A cytologist measured the five different chromosomes in a root-tip cell of a plant (micrometres).

| Chromosome | Short arm | Long arm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 11 |
| 2 | 8 | 8 |
| 3 | 3 | 13 |
